sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Curcumin is the principal yellow pigment in turmeric. Food-grade E100 is a concentrated extract containing curcumin and related pigments. It adds yellow to orange colour to foods. The specified material is supplied as yellow powder or crystalline material.

sections.title: Side effects
paragraphs: At food-use exposures, EFSA retained its ADI; its 2014 assessment nevertheless estimated that some high-consuming toddlers and children could reach or exceed it. These are exposure estimates, not observed symptoms.
At high experimental doses, reduced weight gain in second-generation rats was the endpoint used to set the ADI. This animal evidence does not establish the same effect at ordinary human food intakes.

sections.title: Uses
paragraphs: Examples in the EU food-use list include certain other confectionery including breath freshening microsweets; chewing gum; decorations, coatings and fillings, except fruit-based fillings covered by category 4.2.4; flavoured drinks; flavoured fermented milk products including heat-treated products; unripened cheese excluding products falling in category 16.
The entries apply to particular food categories and may limit the amount, the preparation or the way it is used; they do not show how often the additive appears in retail products.

sections.title: Origin
paragraphs: Plant-derived. Ground turmeric rhizomes are extracted with solvents, and the extract is crystallised to concentrate the colouring compounds.

sections.title: Daily intake
paragraphs: 0–3 mg/kg body weight per day (JECFA, 2003); 3 mg/kg body weight per day (EFSA, 2010).

sections.title: Dietary restrictions
paragraphs: The pigment is extracted from turmeric, a plant, so the pigment itself is compatible with vegan and vegetarian diets.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Turmeric colour is the ground rhizome of Curcuma longa, the same plant material used as a spice. It contains a mixture of plant constituents rather than only the isolated curcumin pigment. FDA defines this preparation separately from turmeric oleoresin and allows its use to colour foods under manufacturing and food-standard conditions. Its food role can therefore involve both the colour and the flavour of the ground spice.

sections.title: Uses
paragraphs: Used as a spice in foods such as curries and mustard. FDA permits turmeric as a colour in foods generally, subject to standards of identity and good manufacturing practice.

sections.title: Origin
paragraphs: Plant-derived. The colour material described by FDA is made by grinding turmeric rhizomes.

sections.title: Daily intake
paragraphs: No ADI allocated for turmeric (JECFA, 1986). JECFA noted that turmeric is often treated as a food rather than a food additive.

sections.title: Dietary restrictions
paragraphs: Ground turmeric is a plant ingredient and is compatible with vegan and vegetarian diets.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Riboflavin is vitamin B2 and a yellow food colour. It occurs naturally in foods and can also be added as a nutrient. Its colour use is covered by E101(i) in the EU specifications. The specified material is supplied as yellow powder or crystalline material.

sections.title: Side effects

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Tartrazine is a manufactured azo dye that gives food a yellow colour. It is sold in the US as FD&C Yellow No. 5. Food-grade material is a purified salt mixture meeting colour specifications. The specified material is supplied as powder or granules.

sections.title: Side effects
paragraphs: At food-use levels, EFSA reported intolerance reactions in a small fraction of people; reactions can occur within the ADI. Studies of colour mixtures with sodium benzoate do not establish that tartrazine alone causes behavioural changes.
At high experimental doses, reduced body weight in rats was the endpoint for JECFA's 2016 ADI. This animal evidence does not establish the same effect at food-use levels in humans.

sections.title: Uses
paragraphs: Examples in the EU food-use list include certain other confectionery including breath freshening microsweets; chewing gum; decorations, coatings and fillings, except fruit-based fillings covered by category 4.2.4; flavoured drinks; flavoured fermented milk products including heat-treated products; unripened cheese excluding products falling in category 16.
The entries apply to particular food categories and may limit the amount, the preparation or the way it is used; they do not show how often the additive appears in retail products.

sections.title: Origin
paragraphs: Synthetic. An aromatic sulfonic acid is diazotised, coupled to a pyrazole compound, and the dye is purified as its sodium salt.

sections.title: Daily intake
paragraphs: 0–10 mg/kg body weight per day (JECFA, 2016). EFSA retained 7.5 mg/kg body weight per day in 2009; these are distinct assessments.

sections.title: Precautions

paragraphs: Quinoline Yellow WS is a yellow food dye based on sulfonated quinophthalone compounds. It is a mixture of colouring salts rather than a single pure molecule. Its role in food is to supply yellow colour. The specified material is supplied as yellow powder or granules.

paragraphs: At food-use levels, EFSA could not firmly attribute reported intolerance reactions to this dye because the evidence was limited. Its 2015 assessment estimated exposure below the ADI after EU use limits were reduced.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Cochineal extract and carmine are red colours whose main pigment is carminic acid. Carmine is a metal complex made from that pigment. In foods these materials produce red shades. The specified material is supplied as deep red powder or liquid.

sections.title: Side effects
paragraphs: At food-use levels, allergic reactions to cochineal/carmine can occur; EFSA could not establish a threshold dose for allergy. Residual proteins were identified as a reason to improve purification.
The animal toxicity studies reviewed by EFSA did not justify lowering the existing ADI; this does not remove the separate allergy risk.

sections.title: Uses
paragraphs: Examples in the EU food-use list include certain other confectionery including breath freshening microsweets; chewing gum; decorations, coatings and fillings, except fruit-based fillings covered by category 4.2.4; flavoured drinks; flavoured fermented milk products including heat-treated products; unripened cheese excluding products falling in category 16.
The entries apply to particular food categories and may limit the amount, the preparation or the way it is used; they do not show how often the additive appears in retail products.

sections.title: Origin
paragraphs: Animal-derived, specifically from dried female cochineal insects. Extraction releases carminic acid; reaction with aluminium forms carmine, sometimes with other metal ions.

sections.title: Daily intake
paragraphs: 2.5 mg carminic acid/kg body weight per day (EFSA, 2015). This expresses the earlier 5 mg carmine/kg body weight ADI in terms of carminic acid content.

sections.title: Dietary restrictions
paragraphs: Not suitable for vegan or vegetarian diets because the colour is extracted from insects.

sections.title: Precautions
paragraphs: EFSA identified allergenic material in E120 and recommended manufacturing purification steps because no allergy threshold could be established.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Citrus Red No. 2 is a synthetic azo dye whose principal component is a dimethoxyphenylazo naphthol compound. Its US food application is unusually narrow: colouring the skin of mature oranges not intended for processing, with the stated packinghouse exception. The limit is 2 mg/kg calculated from the weight of the whole fruit. It is not a general-purpose colour for drinks, sweets or other citrus products under that regulation.

sections.title: Side effects
paragraphs: Human effects at the restricted food-use level were not established in the reviewed JECFA monograph.

Animal studies reviewed in 1969 reported bladder changes and other toxicity at experimental doses, with inconsistent tumour findings. JECFA considered the unexplained results sufficient to reject food-additive use; this is not proof of cancer at the permitted orange-skin exposure.

sections.title: Uses
paragraphs: US authorization covers the skins of mature oranges not intended for processing, with a limit of 2 mg/kg calculated on the whole fruit.

sections.title: Daily intake
paragraphs: No safe intake determined; JECFA concluded that this colour should not be used as a food additive (1969).

sections.title: Overview

sections.title: Side effects
paragraphs: The bodies reached different food-use conclusions: EFSA could not rule out DNA damage in 2021, while FDA reports that JECFA's 2023 evaluation found food use safe.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Sorbic acid is an organic carboxylic acid used for preservative applications in food. Its preservative function is to slow microbial spoilage during storage. The food-grade material is supplied as a white powder or crystals, with purity requirements defining the suitable preparation. Permitted food categories and concentration limits depend on the jurisdiction and the particular food.

sections.title: Uses
paragraphs: Examples in the EU food-use list include certain other confectionery including breath freshening microsweets; chewing gum; decorations, coatings and fillings, except fruit-based fillings covered by category 4.2.4; fruit juices as defined by Directive 2001/112/EC and vegetable juices; flavoured fermented milk products including heat-treated products; unripened cheese excluding products falling in category 16.
The entries apply to particular food categories and may limit the amount, the preparation or the way it is used; they do not show how often the additive appears in retail products.

sections.title: Daily intake
paragraphs: 0-25 mg/kg body weight (JECFA, 1973). This is a combined sorbic-acid and sorbate limit, expressed as sorbic acid.

paragraphs: Butylated hydroxytoluene, usually abbreviated BHT, is a defined phenolic antioxidant. sections.title: Side effects
paragraphs: Mean food-use estimates were below EFSA's limit.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Lecithins are mixtures or fractions of phospholipids from edible plant or animal materials; the specifications also cover suitable enzyme-hydrolysed preparations. Its emulsifying role is to help form or maintain mixtures of oil and water in the finished food. Phospholipid mixtures are separated from vegetable or animal food materials. Some lecithins are further processed with enzymes. The specified material is supplied as brown powder or liquid.

sections.title: Side effects
paragraphs: EFSA found no concern from reported food uses or their associated choline exposure.

sections.title: Uses

paragraphs: Examples in the EU food-use list include certain cocoa and Chocolate products as covered by Directive 2000/36/EC; other confectionery including breath freshening microsweets; chewing gum; decorations, coatings and fillings, except fruit-based fillings covered by category 4.2.4; fruit juices as defined by Directive 2001/112/EC and vegetable juices; flavoured fermented milk products including heat-treated products.
The entries apply to particular food categories and may limit the amount, the preparation or the way it is used; they do not show how often the additive appears in retail products.

sections.title: Daily intake
paragraphs: No ADI specified (JECFA, 1979).

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Metatartaric acid is an esterified material derived from tartaric acid; its chemical form changes as it hydrolyses in water. Its emulsifying role is to help form or maintain mixtures of oil and water in the finished food. The specified material is supplied as white powder or crystalline material. The specification identifies water solubility as one of its properties.

sections.title: Side effects

The assessment assumes conversion to L-tartaric acid before systemic exposure.

sections.title: Uses

sections.title: Overview

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Gum ghatti is a tree-exudate gum also called Indian gum. It comes from wounds in the bark of Anogeissus latifolia and forms viscous preparations in water. Its food role includes emulsifying ingredients so that dispersed components remain mixed. FDA specifies use in non-alcoholic beverages and beverage bases, with a different maximum for other food categories. The source tree and gum identity distinguish it from gum arabic and other plant gums.

sections.title: Uses
paragraphs: An emulsifier in non-alcoholic beverages and beverage bases, with a US maximum of 0.2% in the served food. The FDA regulation sets a 0.1% maximum for other food categories.

sections.title: Origin
paragraphs: Plant-derived exudate collected from wounds in the bark of Anogeissus latifolia, a tree found in India and Sri Lanka.

sections.title: Daily intake
paragraphs: No ADI specified (JECFA, 2017).

sections.title: Dietary restrictions
paragraphs: The gum itself is plant derived and compatible with vegan and vegetarian diets. This origin does not establish halal or kosher certification of a commercial preparation.

paragraphs: E420 covers sorbitol and sorbitol syrup, which are hydrogenated carbohydrate preparations containing the sugar alcohol D-sorbitol. sections.title: Overview

It provides sweetness when added to the food or used in a table-top sweetener preparation. Specified mannitol can be made by hydrogenating glucose- or fructose-containing solutions, or by fermentation with a suitable Zygosaccharomyces rouxii yeast strain. sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Glycerol, also called glycerine, is a three-carbon alcohol with three hydroxyl groups, used in food for moisture control and other formulation purposes. It provides sweetness when added to the food or used in a table-top sweetener preparation. The specified material is supplied as colourless liquid.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Curdlan is a high-molecular-weight glucose polymer with beta-1,3 linkages. The specified ingredient is produced by bacterial fermentation with Alcaligenes faecalis var. myxogenes. FDA describes it as a formulation aid, stabiliser, thickener, texturiser or processing aid. These are preparation-specific technological uses of the carbohydrate polymer.

sections.title: Origin

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Konjac preparations contain glucomannan, a polysaccharide composed of glucose and mannose from the tuber of Amorphophallus konjac. Its emulsifying role is to help form or maintain mixtures of oil and water in the finished food. Konjac gum and konjac glucomannan are obtained from konjac tubers. Water extraction produces the gum, while washing konjac flour with aqueous ethanol yields the glucomannan preparation. One specified form is supplied as white powder.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Cassia gum is the purified ground seed endosperm of Cassia tora and Cassia obtusifolia, consisting mainly of a galactomannan polysaccharide. sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Peptones are mixtures of amino acids and short protein chains obtained by partial breakdown of proteins. The starting proteins may come from animal tissues, milk, eggs or soy. FDA describes production using suitable enzymes, acids or heat. The ingredient has nutrient, processing-aid and surface-active functions, and its composition depends on the starting protein and treatment.

sections.title: Origin
paragraphs: Produced by partial hydrolysis of proteins using suitable proteolytic enzymes, acids or heat. FDA's permitted starting materials include milk proteins, egg albumin, animal tissue, gelatine and soy protein isolate. Peptones can therefore be plant- or animal-derived, depending on the actual starting protein.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Polysorbate 20 is a mixture of ethoxylated sorbitol-derived esters of lauric acid; its preparation contains approximately 20 oxyethylene units per sorbitol-derived unit. Its emulsifying role is to help form or maintain mixtures of oil and water in the finished food. The preparation is made from partial esters of sorbitol and its anhydrides with lauric acid. The esters are additionally reacted with ethylene oxide. The specified preparation is an oily liquid with a colour between lemon yellow and amber. The specification identifies water solubility as one of its properties.

sections.title: Uses
paragraphs: Examples in the EU food-use list include certain other confectionery including breath freshening microsweets; chewing gum; decorations, coatings and fillings, except fruit-based fillings covered by category 4.2.4; flavoured drinks; flavoured fermented milk products including heat-treated products; sweet baked goods.

sections.title: Origin
paragraphs: Made from partial esters of sorbitol and its anhydrides with lauric acid. The esters are additionally reacted with ethylene oxide. The specification does not identify a single biological source for the fatty acid.

sections.title: Dietary restrictions

paragraphs: Pectins are plant-derived polysaccharides consisting mainly of partially methylated polygalacturonic acid; E440 also includes amidated pectins. sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Gelatine is a mixture of animal-derived proteins obtained by partially breaking down collagen. It absorbs water and softens in cold water, then dissolves when heated. On cooling, the solution forms a gel, which explains its gelling function in food. JECFA also identifies stabilising, emulsifying and crystallisation-control functions. The commercial ingredient can be supplied as sheets, flakes or powder, with grades that differ in gel strength.

sections.title: Origin
paragraphs: Gelatine is manufactured by partially hydrolysing collagen from animal tissues such as skin, tendons, ligaments and bones. The protein is extracted and processed into dried sheets, flakes or powder. It is an animal-derived ingredient; the specification does not identify a single animal species for every product.

sections.title: Daily intake
paragraphs: ADI classified as not limited (JECFA, 1970).

sections.title: Dietary restrictions
paragraphs: Ordinary gelatine is made from animal collagen and is therefore unsuitable for vegan and vegetarian diets. Halal and kosher suitability depend on the animal species, slaughter and processing arrangements, and product certification; the E code alone does not establish those conditions.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Brominated vegetable oil is vegetable oil chemically modified with bromine. It was used to keep citrus flavouring dispersed in some drinks, helping the flavouring phase remain mixed with the beverage. Its preparation is distinct from unmodified vegetable oil and from other emulsifying ingredients. FDA revoked its US food-use regulation in 2024, with the compliance date in 2025. The former beverage application is therefore a historical use in the United States.

sections.title: Side effects
paragraphs: FDA concluded that the intended food use could no longer be considered safe after reviewing new studies.
The animal findings indicated potential human health effects; they do not quantify a clinical risk from an individual serving.

sections.title: Origin
paragraphs: Made by modifying vegetable oil with bromine. Its starting oil is plant derived and chemically processed.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Sucrose acetate isobutyrate is a mixture of sucrose esters containing acetate and isobutyrate groups, produced by reacting sucrose with the corresponding anhydrides. Its emulsifying role is to help form or maintain mixtures of oil and water in the finished food. The specified preparation is a pale, straw-coloured liquid. The specification describes it as effectively insoluble in water.

sections.title: Side effects
paragraphs: Assessed food-use estimates were below the limit.
Animal chronic and reproductive studies found no effects at the highest tested dose used to derive the limit.

sections.title: Uses
paragraphs: Examples in the EU food-use list include certain flavoured drinks; other alcoholic beverages including mixtures of alcoholic beverages with non-alcoholic beverages and other alcoholic beverages based on distilled alcohol with alcoholic strength by volume less than 15 %.
The entries apply to particular food categories and may limit the amount, the preparation or the way it is used; they do not show how often the additive appears in retail products.

sections.title: Origin
paragraphs: Chemically manufactured from food-grade sucrose reacted with acetic and isobutyric anhydrides, followed by distillation. The final ingredient is an ester mixture.

sections.title: Daily intake
paragraphs: 20 mg/kg body weight/day (EFSA, 2016).

sections.title: Overview

Its specified function is to help emulsify shortenings and edible oils used in bakery preparations. FDA lists cakes, cake mixes, fillings, icings, pastries and toppings for this application.

sections.title: Origin

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Beta-cyclodextrin is a cyclic carbohydrate containing seven glucose units, manufactured by an enzyme-mediated conversion of starch. Its emulsifying role is to help form or maintain mixtures of oil and water in the finished food. Made by treating partially hydrolysed starch with a microbial cycloglycosyltransferase enzyme. The product consists of rings containing seven glucose units. The specified material is supplied as white crystalline material or solid. Only a limited amount dissolves in water, according to the specification.

sections.title: Side effects
paragraphs: Refined food-use estimates exceeded the limit for several groups.
The reviewed animal studies did not indicate genotoxicity or cancer; the limit incorporates a safety margin.

sections.title: Uses

sections.title: Origin

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: E460 covers microcrystalline and powdered cellulose, both derived from fibrous plant material but processed in different ways. Its emulsifying role is to help form or maintain mixtures of oil and water in the finished food. Cellulose pulp comes from fibrous plant material. Microcrystalline cellulose is purified and partly broken down with mineral acid, while powdered cellulose is purified and mechanically reduced. One specified form is supplied as white powder.

sections.title: Side effects
paragraphs: Assessed food uses raised no concern.
High-dose animal studies found no reproductive or developmental harm.

sections.title: Uses
paragraphs: Examples in the EU food-use list include certain cocoa and Chocolate products as covered by Directive 2000/36/EC; other confectionery including breath freshening microsweets; chewing gum; decorations, coatings and fillings, except fruit-based fillings covered by category 4.2.4; fruit juices as defined by Directive 2001/112/EC and vegetable juices; flavoured fermented milk products including heat-treated products.
The entries apply to particular food categories and may limit the amount, the preparation or the way it is used; they do not show how often the additive appears in retail products.

sections.title: Origin

sections.title: Daily intake
paragraphs: No numerical ADI needed (EFSA, 2018).

sections.title: Dietary restrictions
paragraphs: The specified starting material is plant derived and compatible with vegetarian and vegan diets. The specification does not establish halal or kosher certification.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: E472 is a group label for acid esters of mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids. The specified subgroups use acetic, lactic, citric or tartaric acids, including acetylated-tartaric and mixed-acid preparations. The precise suffix identifies the preparation, so the group name alone is insufficient to assign one composition or intake assessment.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Succinylated monoglycerides are mixtures of succinic-acid esters of mono- and diglycerides. The starting glycerides are made from edible fats or oils, or by directly esterifying glycerol with food fatty acids. FDA describes use as an emulsifier in shortening and as a dough conditioner in bread manufacture. These applications have different concentration limits, and the starting fat source is not fixed by the name.

sections.title: Uses
paragraphs: Used as an emulsifier in liquid or plastic shortenings and as a dough conditioner in bread baking. The US maxima are 3% of shortening weight and 0.5% of flour weight, respectively, subject to the relevant food standards.

sections.title: Origin
paragraphs: Produced by adding succinic-acid ester groups to mono- and diglycerides. FDA describes glyceride starting materials made either from edible fats and oils or by reacting glycerol with food fatty acids. The particular fat or fatty-acid source is not fixed by this definition.

sections.title: Daily intake
paragraphs: No ADI allocated (JECFA, 1982).

The specified material is supplied as white powder or solid. Only a limited amount dissolves in water, according to the specification.

sections.title: Overview

Its emulsifying role is to help form or maintain mixtures of oil and water in the finished food. The specified material is supplied as white powder. sections.title: Overview

JECFA describes the material as a heterogeneous residual preparation, so it should not be equated with every purified calcium-phosphate salt. Its listed functions include emulsifying, retaining moisture and binding metal ions. The historical entry describes the bone-phosphate preparation specifically, while related phosphates have separate identities.

This historical entry is retained separately from the current E452 grouped designation. A precise food-use or intake claim must identify the preparation covered by its source.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Ammonium polyphosphate is an ammonium salt preparation of polyphosphoric acid. Its phosphate units can form chains and branched structures, and the chain length influences its water solubility and other physical properties. It can be made by reacting concentrated phosphoric acid with ammonia. This historical entry gives an emulsifying classification. The general chemical name does not identify one food-grade composition or a typical current human-food application.

sections.title: Overview

sections.title: Overview

Its proposed technological use is to reduce caking in animal feed. The mineral mixture and source deposit are part of the identity of the preparation assessed.

sections.title: Origin
paragraphs: Mineral-derived. The assessed preparation is made from volcanic rock quarried in the Kaiserstuhl area of Germany, then crushed, milled, conditioned at 350 to 400 degrees Celsius and finely ground.

sections.title: Precautions
paragraphs: EFSA could not conclude on target-animal safety of the assessed natrolite-phonolite feed preparation in 2023. Risks associated with possible nanoparticles could not be assessed for animals, consumers or users; handling also raised sensitisation concerns. These findings concern the specified feed material and do not establish a typical direct human-food use.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: 4-Hexylresorcinol is an organic resorcinol derivative used to control browning in crustaceans. Its food application is prevention of melanosis, the darkening that can develop in shrimps and related crustaceans. EFSA assessed that particular antioxidant use in 2014. The accepted application is linked to a residue limit in crustacean meat, rather than unrestricted use as an antioxidant throughout foods.

sections.title: Side effects
paragraphs: At the assessed food exposure: EFSA considered the margin between estimated dietary exposure and the experimental toxicity benchmark sufficient for the limited shrimp and crustacean application in 2014. This was a regulatory assessment, not evidence from a trial showing that every exposure has no effects.

At higher experimental exposure: mouse studies identified kidney damage as the most sensitive toxicity endpoint. EFSA found the data inadequate for an ADI and required additional reproductive-toxicity data before any expansion of use.

sections.title: Uses
paragraphs: Used to prevent melanosis, or darkening, in shrimps and related crustaceans. EFSA's 2014 assessment accepted this limited use provided residues in crustacean meat did not exceed 2 mg/kg.

sections.title: Daily intake
paragraphs: No ADI established because the available database was insufficient (EFSA, 2014). EFSA accepted the limited crustacean application with residues not exceeding 2 mg/kg in crustacean meat; this residue limit is not a daily intake limit.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Perlite is a naturally occurring aluminosilicate volcanic-glass material. EFSA's 2025 assessment concerns a preparation containing predominantly expanded perlite, with limits on crystalline mineral components. The material is supplied as powder or granules and is intended to reduce caking in animal feed. Its mineral composition and physical form matter to that handling function. The reviewed feed preparation does not establish a typical direct use in human food.

sections.title: Origin
paragraphs: Mineral-derived perlite from a natural deposit. The assessed feed product is predominantly expanded aluminosilicate volcanic glass; the public assessment does not disclose the complete processing method.

sections.title: Precautions
paragraphs: EFSA's 2025 assessment identified skin and respiratory sensitisation concerns for handlers of the specified perlite feed preparation. Safety conclusions for the animals applied to particular tested or extrapolated categories, with no conclusion for the remaining categories. These findings concern the evaluated feed product, rather than reported reactions from direct food use.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Amylases are enzymes that break down starch into smaller carbohydrate molecules. This entry names an enzyme family rather than one production strain or commercial preparation. For example, FDA describes an alpha-amylase obtained by fermentation of Bacillus stearothermophilus for making maltodextrins and nutritive carbohydrate sweeteners. The enzyme acts during processing; its source organism and preparation specifications remain relevant to the particular ingredient.

sections.title: Uses
paragraphs: The specified bacterial alpha-amylase is used during starch processing to produce maltodextrins and nutritive carbohydrate sweeteners.

sections.title: Origin
paragraphs: Production depends on the amylase preparation. One FDA-specified alpha-amylase is recovered from the culture filtrate of a pure bacterial fermentation using Bacillus stearothermophilus.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Proteases are enzymes that split peptide bonds in proteins. This entry includes papain from papaya, bromelain from pineapple and ficin from fig-plant latex, as well as other protease preparations. FDA also describes bacterial proteases obtained by fermentation of specified Bacillus strains. Their technological action is protein breakdown, with the resulting effect depending on the food process and enzyme preparation. An evaluation of one source or enzyme cannot describe every member of the family.

sections.title: Uses
paragraphs: Protease applications depend on the enzyme preparation. FDA's specified mixed bacterial carbohydrase-protease preparation is used in alcoholic beverages, candy, nutritive sweeteners and protein hydrolysates.

sections.title: Origin
paragraphs: The named plant preparations include papain from papaya latex, bromelain from pineapple and ficin from fig-tree latex. Other specified proteases are microbial preparations recovered from bacterial fermentation.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Glucose oxidase is an enzyme that oxidises glucose using oxygen and produces glucono-delta-lactone and hydrogen peroxide. It occurs in several biological sources, including certain fungi. Its biochemical reaction is distinct from simply adding a small-molecule antioxidant. Food-processing activity depends on the availability of glucose and oxygen and on the particular enzyme preparation. The general identity source does not establish one commercial production strain or a typical current finished-food example.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Invertase is a sucrose-hydrolysing enzyme produced from Saccharomyces cerevisiae yeast. Its stabilising role is to help a food maintain its physical consistency or the distribution of its ingredients. Produced from the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae. The recovered material is an enzyme preparation.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Lipases are enzymes that act on fats, including the hydrolysis of fatty-acid glycerides. FDA describes animal lipases extracted from edible stomach or pancreatic tissues and a separate preparation produced by fermentation of Rhizopus niveus. A further specified fungal esterase-lipase is used for flavour development in cheese, fats, oils and milk products. The source, carrier and reaction activity differ between preparations. Consequently, this family name alone does not identify the origin or dietary suitability of a commercial enzyme.

sections.title: Uses
paragraphs: Specified lipase preparations are used in fat and oil processing. The fungal esterase-lipase described in 21 CFR 173.140 has flavour-enhancing applications in certain cheeses, fats, oils and milk products.

sections.title: Origin
paragraphs: Source-dependent. FDA describes extracts of edible calf, kid or lamb stomach tissues or pancreatic tissues, as well as separate fungal-fermentation preparations. These are distinct commercial enzyme types.

sections.title: Dietary restrictions
paragraphs: Animal-tissue lipases are not suitable for vegans or vegetarians. A microbial source alone does not establish suitability of the whole preparation: the FDA-specified fungal esterase-lipase can use sweet whey as its carrier. Halal and kosher status depends on the particular source, carrier and certification.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Lysozyme is an enzyme protein obtained from hens' egg white; it breaks bonds in bacterial cell-wall material, particularly in Gram-positive bacteria. Its preservative role is to limit spoilage caused by microorganisms and extend the storage life of the food. Obtained from hen egg white, usually as the hydrochloride salt. It is an animal-derived enzyme protein. The specified material is supplied as white powder.

sections.title: Uses

sections.title: Dietary restrictions

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Dextrins are starch carbohydrates whose chains have been partly broken down. FDA describes manufacture by dry heating several edible starches, sometimes after treatment with suitable acids or alkalis. sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Alkaline-treated starch is food starch modified by treatment with sodium hydroxide or potassium hydroxide. JECFA describes this treatment as causing limited fragmentation of the original starch structure. The preparation has thickening, stabilising, binding or emulsifying functions. Non-pregelatinised material retains starch granules and is insoluble in cold water but develops a viscous dispersion in hot water. The modification is distinct from acetylation or phosphate crosslinking.

sections.title: Origin
